body.text: For Kazakhstan, a country linking China and Europe while sharing a long border with Russia, infrastructure is never entirely a domestic matter. Railways determine how goods move across Eurasia, electricity supplies shape industrial investment, and the ability to process minerals affects the country’s place in international supply chains. These connections offer a useful way to read President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s October 28 State of the Nation address, which was mostly about economic development but had also important implications for foreign relations.

Tokayev began by warning of deepening mistrust among major powers and a more unpredictable international environment. Rather than proposing a new diplomatic alignment, he emphasized a stronger economy, modern infrastructure, technology, and effective institutions. For Kazakhstan’s longstanding balanced and multivector foreign policy, the underlying logic is that domestic capacity can widen the scope for cooperation with different partners at the same time.

The most visible proposal was the nationwide “People’s Construction” program, backed by 6.5 trillion tenge (approximately $14 billion) from the National Fund through 2029, including 1.5 trillion tenge earmarked for early social projects. Roads, utilities, housing, and public facilities are central to the plan. Tokayev also proposed a higher minimum wage and new healthcare facilities. These measures principally address domestic needs, but more reliable services and regional infrastructure can also reduce costs for investors and make industrial projects more viable outside the largest cities. The president’s insistence that public spending mobilize private capital, rather than substitute for it, gives the initiative an international dimension.

The clearest connection between domestic investment and foreign relations is transport. Tokayev said the Bakhty-Ayagoz railway should enter service in 2027, adding 20 million tons of capacity on routes toward China. Construction has also begun on an Aral-Caspian corridor intended to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by roughly 1,000 kilometers. Both projects respond to an established demand for more dependable links between Asian production centers and European markets. In February, the World Bank approved an $846 million guarantee designed to mobilize $1.41 billion in commercial financing for Kazakhstan’s rail network along the Middle Corridor.

The geopolitical value of these routes lies in their usefulness to multiple economies. China gains additional westward capacity, European businesses gain another option for moving goods, and Kazakhstan can expand its role in services surrounding that trade. Tokayev’s call for freight consolidation centers, logistics operators, and factories near transport junctions suggests an ambition to capture value beyond transit fees. Yet the route’s performance will depend not only on Kazakh construction but also on ports, customs procedures and coordination with Azerbaijan, Georgia, and other corridor partners. Greater connectivity is a regional undertaking, not simply a national project.

The same logic applies to data. On October 15, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan inaugurated a 380-kilometer fiber-optic link beneath the Caspian Sea, designed to carry information between Central Asia and Europe. Mentioned again in the address, the cable shows how physical and digital connectivity can reinforce one another. Reliable cross-border data links matter to cloud services, financial transactions, and the data centers Kazakhstan wants to attract.

China’s role is notable in other spheres too. At a September China-Kazakhstan investment forum, Tokayev described a portfolio of 260 joint industrial projects valued at more than $62 billion, spanning manufacturing, metallurgy, agriculture, and energy storage. Its composition indicates how the relationship is developing from commodity trade and transport toward local production and technology. The address’s emphasis on manufacturing capacity and domestic suppliers is consistent with this direction.

Energy provides a second intersection between internal requirements and external partnerships. Kazakhstan generates about 123 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually but still faces shortages. Tokayev set a goal of achieving a sustained surplus by 2029 through new generation, modernized grids and a broader mix of energy sources. Russia is an established partner in this sector. During President Vladimir Putin’s May visit, the two countries signed a nuclear power agreement and arrangements for Russian export-credit financing. Chinese companies have also proposed nuclear cooperation, including technology transfer and specialist training, as Tokayev noted in the address.

These projects are significant because a nuclear partnership can encompass engineering, fuel services, training and maintenance over decades. They should not, however, be mistaken for an immediate solution to the 2029 electricity target: the first planned reactor is not expected to begin operating before the following decade. In the nearer term, grid upgrades and other generation projects will remain decisive. For Kazakhstan’s partners, a more dependable power system would also improve the prospects for energy-intensive manufacturing, mineral processing and computing infrastructure.

Critical minerals offer another area in which domestic reforms can produce international effects. Tokayev called for modern geological exploration, better access to geological data, long-term financing and offtake arrangements, alongside consideration of a dedicated mechanism for nonferrous and rare-earth metals. The objective is to develop processing and other parts of industrial value chains. This meets interests expressed by both Western and Asian partners, although turning resource potential into competitive production will require technology, investment and skills.

During Tokayev’s June visit to Brussels, EU leaders identified critical raw materials, energy, transport and digitalization as priorities for expanded cooperation. As Kazakhstan’s largest trading and investment partner, the EU has a particularly strong interest in the development of these sectors. The United States and Kazakhstan have also agreed to cooperate on mineral supply chains, including a proposed American-backed tungsten mining and processing project. These relationships have distinct commercial purposes, but each could support Kazakhstan’s stated goal of producing more value domestically. They complement its established energy and industrial ties with Russia and China rather than necessarily displacing them.

Technology is becoming a further point of international engagement. The address highlighted two operating supercomputers, another planned before year’s end, and efforts to apply artificial intelligence to agriculture, industry and public services. In June, Kazakhstan joined the U.S.-backed Pax Silica initiative and signed an AI Opportunity Partnership statement, connecting cooperation on computing, semiconductors, energy, critical minerals and research. On October 23, Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana and met Tokayev. Nvidia’s own account of the visit described planned computing investments and potential applications in mining, agriculture and industrial automation. These developments give the digital agenda a tangible international dimension, although the economic benefits will depend on adoption by ordinary businesses as much as high-profile infrastructure.

The final link is institutional. Tokayev acknowledged weaknesses in investment coordination and proposed a larger role for the Baiterek development holding, a new civil code, adjustments to tax rules and an English common law-based investment court in Alatau. Such changes will matter to foreign partners only insofar as they create predictable conditions in practice. The same is true of financing: public construction spending can initiate projects, but sustained industrial cooperation requires viable businesses, long-term credit and confidence in dispute resolution.

The address did not signify a departure from Kazakhstan’s established diplomatic approach. It suggests rather how that approach might acquire greater economic substance. China’s industrial and transport links, Russia’s energy cooperation, the EU’s connectivity and raw-materials partnerships, and emerging U.S. ties in minerals and artificial intelligence each intersect with priorities set out by Tokayev. Delivery remains the essential test. If infrastructure is completed, power becomes more reliable and investment rules improve, Kazakhstan could become a stronger participant in the production, services and technology networks that connect Eurasia.
